shapes.guarded_twin: The same literal with an `f` prefix, or an explicit `.format(...)` on it. Both twins are usually present elsewhere in the same file, because the author writes far more of them correctly than not.
shapes.hunt: For each instance, check every other message in the same module for the same slip -- a codebase that drops one `f` drops several, and they cluster in rarely-executed branches (a platform fallback, an unreachable `else`, an error path) because a formatted message would have been noticed the first time anyone saw it. Grep the whole tree for a brace field in a message argument, then apply the differential below.
shapes.expected: the reader sees the value the field names, not the field.
shapes.caught_as: COMPLETELY SILENT. It is not an error to have braces in a string; the message simply renders wrong. It surfaces only when a human reads the output, which for an error path may be never.
confirmed_examples: CPython Lib/test/test_tarfile.py:3871 -- `raise NotImplementedError("Need to guess component length for {sys.platform}")`, in the `else` branch of a platform check. The ONLY finding across 1,847 files of CPython's Lib/, with zero false positives.
references: str.format / format string syntax: replacement fields are only substituted by str.format, str.format_map, or an f-string prefix

Calibrated over CPython Lib/ (1,847 files): 4 raw candidates, 1 after the three-part differential, 0 false positives. idlelib, _pyrepl and coverage.py each produce 0, so the shape adds no false-positive pressure to the benchmarks.
shapes.differential: Three filters carry this shape, and each corresponds to a real guarded twin. (1) ANY other argument on the call means something may still format the string -- `_pyrepl/trace.py` formats `line.format(*k, **kw)` only `if k or kw`, so `trace('{x}', v)` is correct. (2) A literal that is the RECEIVER of `.format`/`.format_map` is formatted in place -- `runpy.py:125` builds a multi-line braced message and formats it on the spot. (3) Only fields whose name is an IDENTIFIER count: `{}` and `{0}` are indistinguishable from a regex quantifier (`\d{4}`) or a literal brace in a character class, and those two classes alone were 90% of the raw candidates over CPython's `Lib/`. Also skip `${name}`, which is `string.Template` or shell syntax. A template CONSTANT consumed by a formatter elsewhere (`_DEPRECATED_MSG` in `warnings`, `glob._deprecated_function_message`) is the commonest near-miss and is excluded by filter 1 at its call site.

shapes.title: `zip()` without `strict=` silently truncates when the two sides disagree in length
shapes.pattern: `zip(a, b)` where the two operands come from DIFFERENT computations over the same underlying data -- one from arithmetic over an index (`range(...)`, a parsed line number, a slice bound), the other from the data itself (`.splitlines()`, `.readlines()`, a widget query, a directory listing). When they disagree, `zip` stops at the shorter one and the surplus is dropped with no error and no log line.
shapes.guarded_twin: `zip(a, b, strict=True)`, which raises `ValueError` on the first mismatch. The twin is frequently in the project's OWN TESTS for the very function that lacks it -- idlelib's `idle_test/test_sidebar.py:764` passes `strict=True` while `pyshell.py:1002`, the production code it tests, does not.
shapes.hunt: Rank every un-stricted `zip` by whether the operands share a derivation. Same expression on both sides, or two calls with an identical count argument, are structurally equal -- skip them. Escalate when one side comes from `range()`/`int()`/a slice bound and the other from a split, a read, or a query. Then grep the tests for the same pairing done with `strict=True`.
shapes.expected: every element of both sequences is consumed; disagreeing lengths are a bug the program surfaces.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- a short file, a missing last row, a clipboard one line short. In test code it is worse than silent: the test still passes, having asserted less than it claims.
confirmed_examples: CPython Lib/idlelib/pyshell.py:1002 -- copy-with-prompts drops the last selected line whenever the selection ends at a column that is a multiple of 10; verified against a live tkinter.Text
CPython Lib/idlelib/idle_test/test_searchbase.py:122,134 -- zip(declared_options, actually_packed_widgets); a dialog packing too few buttons would pass vacuously
references: PEP 618 -- Add Optional Length-Checking To zip
ruff B905 / flake8-bugbear
shapes.differential: Do NOT report when both operands are provably equal-length: a list zipped against a comprehension over it, `zip(x[::2], x[1::2])` over a contract-even sequence, or two generators sharing a count argument. Ragged truncation must be REACHABLE, not merely unproven. Conversely a `zip` in a test pairing EXPECTED against ACTUAL is worth flagging even when currently balanced -- there truncation silently weakens the assertion, which is `test-cannot-fail` arriving by another route.

shapes.title: A validity guard ANDed with a preference flag, so turning the preference off removes the guard
shapes.pattern: An early return that combines a validity test with a configuration flag governing only a side effect: `if value is None and self.NOTIFY: notify(); return`. Turn the preference off and the guard disappears entirely, letting the invalid value reach code that dereferences it. It reads correctly because the null test IS present and the preference defaults to on -- so the bug is unreachable in every default configuration and in every test.
shapes.guarded_twin: Split the conjunction: the guard unconditional, only the side effect optional. Sibling callers in the same module almost always already return unconditionally on their own None conditions.
shapes.hunt: Grep `if <null/validity test> and <FLAG>:` and its mirror, where FLAG is a module/class constant, a settings lookup, or a name matching BELL/VERBOSE/WARN/NOTIFY/DEBUG/QUIET/STRICT. Ask what the flag controls: a NOTIFICATION conjoined with a VALIDITY condition is the shape. Then flip the flag off and re-trace every consumer past the guard for a subscript or attribute access.
shapes.expected: the invalid value is rejected on every path; the preference only decides whether the user is told.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT under every default configuration, then a hard TypeError/AttributeError once the preference is changed -- reported as 'turning off the bell broke bracket matching', which points at the notification rather than the guard.
confirmed_examples: CPython Lib/idlelib/parenmatch.py:97 -- `if indices is None and self.BELL:`; unchecking 'Bell on Mismatch' makes an unmatched bracket raise TypeError out of a Tk callback and leaves the restore bindings registered
shapes.differential: Not this shape when both conjuncts are data conditions, nor when the flag selects a different valid behaviour rather than a notification. Discriminator: does the code after the guard tolerate the value the guard was testing for? If it dereferences it, the conjunction is the bug.

shapes.title: A per-element property computed once from the concatenated whole, then applied to every element
shapes.pattern: A property that belongs to each ELEMENT -- a comment prefix, an indent width, a field separator, a record header -- is derived once from the joined value (`header = get_header('\n'.join(lines))`) and applied to all of them. An anchored regex or a `split()[0]` answers for element one only; the consumer then does `line[len(header):]` on every element, so each one that lacked the property loses that many leading characters.
shapes.guarded_twin: The sibling path that ESTABLISHES the invariant before relying on it -- typically a loop extending the region only while `get_header(line) == header`. That twin usually exists in the same module for the auto-detect case, with the bug living in the explicit/user-supplied-range case.
shapes.hunt: Find every helper named or documented for a single line/record and grep its call sites for one passing a joined or multi-line value. Then check whether the consumer applies the result per-element. Reproduce with a two-element input whose first element has the property and the second does not -- the shape is invisible on homogeneous input, which is why every test passes.
shapes.expected: each element is transformed according to its own properties, or the operation refuses a heterogeneous region.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT DATA LOSS. Nothing raises; a fixed number of leading characters simply disappears from every non-conforming element, proportional to the first element's prefix length.
confirmed_examples: CPython Lib/idlelib/format.py:57-59 -- Format Paragraph over a selection whose first line is a comment: verified by execution, `result = compute(a, b)` becomes `esult = compute(a, b)` and the result is written back to the buffer
shapes.differential: Fine when the aggregate genuinely has one answer (a file-level encoding, a uniform delimiter). The evidence is an ANCHORED match (`^`) or a first-element pick applied across a multi-element value, plus a consumer that slices by the derived length.

shapes.title: A render-scoped cache read by a consumer that iterates the whole model
shapes.pattern: A dict or list built for RENDERING -- populated only while walking the currently-visible rows, reset on every redraw -- is later read by a consumer that iterates the FULL range and treats a missing key as a legitimate 'no value' (`.get(k)` -> None) rather than as 'not indexed'. The display cache silently doubles as a data model.
shapes.guarded_twin: A consumer that recomputes the property from the underlying model rather than the render cache, or a producer that indexes the whole model and only DRAWS the visible slice.
shapes.hunt: For every attribute assigned inside a paint/redraw/update method, find every reader outside that method. Flag any reader whose key range comes from the full model rather than the same visible window. `.get(k)` with an implicit None default is the strongest tell, because it converts 'absent' into a valid value. Reproduce by making the model taller than the viewport and scrolling before invoking the consumer.
shapes.expected: the consumer sees a value for every element of the model, not only those currently on screen.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT and SCROLL-DEPENDENT. The output is well-formed and merely incomplete, and it is correct whenever the model fits on one screen -- so it survives every small-input test and every interactive check.
confirmed_examples: CPython Lib/idlelib/sidebar.py:466-486 -> pyshell.py:997 -- shell prompts are indexed with `@0,0` + `dlineinfo` (viewport-only) and consumed across the whole buffer on save, so every prompt scrolled off-screen is missing from the saved file
shapes.differential: Not this shape when the consumer's range is itself bounded by the same viewport, nor when a missing key is explicitly distinguished from a null value. The bug requires BOTH the render-scoped producer AND a full-range consumer that cannot tell absent from empty.

shapes.title: A structured index interrogated with a string operation instead of being parsed
shapes.pattern: A value with internal structure -- a Tk text index `line.col`, a dotted version, an `ip:port`, a `path:lineno` -- is tested with `[-1]`, `endswith`, `startswith` or a slice in place of splitting it and comparing the field numerically. The test then agrees with the intended predicate only for a subset of values: `sellast[-1] != '0'` means `column != 0` for single-digit columns and silently means the wrong thing for 10, 20, 100.
shapes.guarded_twin: Parse then compare -- `int(index.split('.')[1]) != 0` -- or use the API's own arithmetic. A correct sibling is usually adjacent: idlelib's own `text.index('sel.first linestart')` on the line above does exactly this for the start index while the end index is tested by suffix.
shapes.hunt: Grep for `[-1] ==`, `[-1] !=`, `.endswith(` and `.startswith(` applied to a variable produced by an index-, version-, address- or location-returning API. For each, ask which values of the underlying FIELD the character test misclassifies; a non-empty reachable set is a defect.
shapes.expected: the predicate holds for every value of the structured field, not only its single-character encodings.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT and PERIODIC -- fails for one value in ten (or one in twenty-six), which reads as an intermittent glitch and is very hard to attribute from a bug report.
confirmed_examples: CPython Lib/idlelib/pyshell.py:1020 -- `if sellast[-1] != '0'` intends `column != 0`; verified against live Tk, selecting to column 10 or 20 drops the last line from the clipboard
references: Tk text index format `line.char`, Tcl/Tk text(n)
shapes.differential: A string test on a genuinely flat string (a file extension, a scheme prefix) is correct and not this shape. The shape requires the value to have a PARSED field the test stands in for. Exclude cases where the field is provably single-character by construction.

shapes.title: A test whose assertion is made against a stub incapable of expressing the failure
shapes.pattern: A test achieves full line coverage of a guarded path while asserting against a mock or stub that can never produce the condition the guard exists for. `self.gui = Mock()` then asserting `interaction` was called proves nothing about a `try/except TclError` around it, because a Mock never raises TclError. Likewise a fake widget whose `index()` is frozen to a constant, or a stub returning a value unconditionally where the real object returns a sentinel.
shapes.guarded_twin: The same test with `side_effect` set to the exception, or a real object in place of the stub. A sibling test in the same file usually already does one or the other.
shapes.hunt: MUTATION-TEST the guarded line: break it and run the suite. A surviving mutant is proof, not a guess. Then look for the stub in the fixture -- `Mock()` with no `side_effect`, a lambda assigned over a method (`cls.text.index = lambda i: '4.0'`), or a fake returning a value unconditionally where the real API can fail. Compare against the real object's contract: which states can it reach that the stub cannot?
shapes.expected: a test covering a guard can distinguish the guarded code from the unguarded code.
shapes.caught_as: NEVER. The test passes, the line is covered, and no coverage tool reports anything. The defect it was meant to catch ships.
confirmed_examples: CPython Lib/idlelib/idle_test/test_debugger.py:53,59 -- both user_line (guarded) and user_exception (unguarded) tested with `self.gui = Mock()`; a Mock never raises TclError, so both pass identically. This is what hid CRF-IDLELIB-0025

CPython Lib/idlelib/idle_test/test_searchengine.py:279 -- `cls.text.index = lambda index: '4.0'` freezes every index expression; two mutations of search_backward's wrap survive the full 623-test suite while the mirrored search_forward mutation kills five tests

CRF-COVPY-0065 -- coverage.py files.py:35: the system-root separator guard, whose only test (test_files.py:93) patches os.path.normcase to return curdir, making its own assertion a tautology. Mutant survives on BOTH tracer cores; the inverse mutant kills 92 tests, proving non-equivalence. Second codebase, and found by mutation rather than reading
shapes.differential: A stub is correct when the test's subject is the CALL, not the guard -- verifying an argument was forwarded needs no ability to raise. The shape requires a guard, branch or sentinel handler whose condition the stub cannot produce. Distinct from `test-cannot-fail`, where the assertion is tautological or absent; here the assertion is real and the FIXTURE is what cannot fail.

shapes.title: A binding, callback, or handle created inside a redraw is never released
shapes.pattern: A render/redraw/refresh routine creates a per-element registration -- a widget event binding, a signal connection, an observer, a scheduled callback, a native handle -- once per element per pass, and there is no matching release. The routine is called again on every expand, scroll, resize or refresh, so registrations accumulate linearly with redraws rather than with elements. Each one usually captures the element, so the retained set pins application objects too.
shapes.guarded_twin: A sibling view in the same package that binds ONCE at construction, or that explicitly unbinds before rebinding. Frameworks that auto-release on widget destruction (Tk deletes a widget's Tcl commands in `Misc.destroy`) make some instances harmless -- the twin worth citing is one that survives destruction of the individual element but not of the container.
shapes.hunt: Find the redraw entry point and every registration call inside it (`tag_bind`, `bind`, `connect`, `addObserver`, `after`, `register`), then grep the whole class for the matching release (`tag_unbind`, `unbind`, `disconnect`, `after_cancel`). Absence of the release verb anywhere in the file is the signal. MEASURE it: drive N redraws and count registrations (in Tk, `len(widget.tk.call('info','commands'))`), and confirm growth is linear in redraws, not in elements.
shapes.expected: registrations track live elements, not cumulative redraws.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT. Nothing raises; the window is simply slower and larger the longer it is open, and the objects it displayed are not collected. Frequently already documented by a stale in-code TODO/XXX that has outlived several maintainers.
confirmed_examples: CRF-IDLELIB-0057 -- idlelib tree.py:234 calls canvas.tag_bind twice per node on every redraw, under a comment reading 'XXX This leaks bindings until canvas is deleted' that has been correct since 1999
references: Tk: bindings created with tag_bind persist until the canvas item or the canvas is destroyed
shapes.differential: Not this shape if the framework releases on element destruction AND elements are destroyed per redraw -- measure before reporting, because that is the common case and it is a non-issue. The real instance is a container that outlives its elements: the container is destroyed rarely (a browser window open for a session) while elements are re-rendered constantly. A long-lived XXX naming the leak is corroboration, not proof; the measurement is the proof.

shapes.title: A debug env flag parsed with bare `int()`, so any non-decimal value crashes import
shapes.pattern: A module-scope toggle read as `bool(int(os.getenv("FLAG", 0)))` or `int(os.environ.get(...))`. The name and the `bool()` say boolean, but the parser accepts only decimal digits, so the spellings a user actually reaches for -- `true`, `yes`, `on`, and the EMPTY STRING that `export FLAG=` produces -- raise `ValueError` at import time, before any of the project's error handling exists.
shapes.guarded_twin: The project's own config layer, which almost always has a checked boolean reader: a `getboolean` that maps `{'true': True, 'false': False}` and raises a contextualised error naming the option and the bad value. The env path bypasses it because it runs at module scope, before the config object exists.
shapes.hunt: Grep for `int(os.getenv` / `int(os.environ` at module scope. For each, TRY THE SPELLINGS: `true`, `yes`, `on`, `1`, and empty. Then ask what swallows the ValueError -- a bare `except:` in a sitecustomize/.pth bootstrap turns the crash into a silent no-op, which is far worse than the crash.
shapes.expected: an unparseable flag is either ignored with a warning or rejected with a message naming the variable.
shapes.caught_as: LOUD as a traceback at import -- unless something upstream swallows it, and for a tool injected via a .pth file or sitecustomize something usually does. Then it is SILENT and the tool simply does not run.
confirmed_examples: CRF-COVPY-0061 -- coverage.py sysmon.py:50,53: COVERAGE_SYSMON_LOG=true, =yes, or empty all raise ValueError from `import coverage`; only `1` works. pth_file.py:13's bare `except:` then swallows it, so subprocesses contribute zero data with no diagnostic
references: A shell `export FLAG=` sets the variable to the empty string, which is the single most likely way a user disables a flag
shapes.differential: Not this shape when the value is genuinely numeric (a timeout, a level, a size) -- that is `unvalidated-numeric-from-environment`. The discriminator is the `bool()` wrapper or a name reading as an on/off toggle: it tells you the author meant a flag and reached for the wrong parser.

shapes.title: A naive `datetime.now()` written into a versioned file format or a public schema
shapes.pattern: `datetime.now().isoformat()` or `.strftime(...)` with no `tz` and no offset in the format, where the result is written into an artifact OTHER PROGRAMS READ -- a versioned JSON report, a documented database column, an export consumed by a dashboard. The timestamp is unanchored, so two runs an hour apart across a DST transition are byte-identical and no consumer can order them.
shapes.guarded_twin: A sibling emitter in the same project that gets it right -- an epoch value, or a helper doing `.astimezone()` with `%z`. When one exists, the fix is an import away and the divergence is the whole argument.
shapes.hunt: Do NOT grep for `datetime.now()` and report the count -- that is a style pass with a terrible hit rate. Follow the value to its DESTINATION and keep only the ones that reach a persisted or exported artifact. Then check the project's other timestamp emitters: if they disagree about offsets, that disagreement is the finding.
shapes.expected: a timestamp leaving the process carries its offset, or is epoch-based.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT, and only near a DST boundary or across machines in different zones -- which is exactly when someone is trying to order two runs to explain a regression.
confirmed_examples: CRF-COVPY-0062 -- coverage.py jsonreport.py:83 emits '2026-07-27T06:25:25.765492' into a FORMAT_VERSION'd JSON report and sqldata.py:368 writes the same shape into the documented `meta.when` column, while the html backend's misc.py:288 format_local_datetime correctly emits '2026-07-27 06:25 -0400'
references: ruff DTZ005 / DTZ006 flag the call site; the destination is what decides whether it matters
shapes.differential: A naive timestamp used only for an in-process duration, a log line, or a filename is fine -- do not report it. The destination is the entire test: it must be read by something outside this process.

shapes.title: A tool reports its own failures through a channel the observed program can switch off
shapes.pattern: An instrumentation tool -- profiler, tracer, coverage measurer, linter plugin -- emits its diagnostics via `warnings.warn`, the `logging` root, or `sys.stdout`, all of which the program being measured owns and reconfigures. Two lines in the subject (`warnings.simplefilter('ignore')`, `logging.disable()`) silence every diagnostic the tool has, including the ones that say its measurement is wrong.
shapes.guarded_twin: A second output path in the same tool that writes straight to `sys.stderr` (or to its own file) and cannot be reconfigured from outside. Its existence proves the author knew some messages must survive -- the finding is that the wrong messages went down the reconfigurable channel.
shapes.hunt: Enumerate every diagnostic the tool can emit and sort them by channel. Then write a subject program that suppresses that channel and re-run: whatever disappears is the list. Weight by severity -- a suppressed 'measurement may be wrong' is far worse than a suppressed 'nothing to do'.
shapes.expected: a tool's statements about its own correctness are not suppressible by the code it is observing.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT, and specifically silent in the situation the diagnostic exists for. Common in CI, where a project sets a global warning filter for its own reasons and unknowingly mutes its coverage tool.
confirmed_examples: CRF-COVPY-0063 -- coverage.py control.py:495 routes all 18 diagnostics through warnings.warn; two lines of warnings.simplefilter('ignore') in the measured program take the CoverageWarning count from 2 to 0, including 'Trace function changed, data is likely wrong'. The twin _message() at :501-504 prints to stderr unconditionally
shapes.differential: Not this shape for a library reporting on ITS CALLER's misuse -- `warnings.warn` is exactly right there, and the caller silencing it is the caller's choice. The shape needs the observer/observed split: the program muting the message is not the program the message is about.

shapes.title: `atexit.register(self.method)` with no `unregister`, pinning the object for the process lifetime
shapes.pattern: An object registers a BOUND METHOD with `atexit` (or `signal`, or a global registry) in its setup path, and nothing ever unregisters it. The bound method holds `self`, so the object and everything it references survive `del` and every collection, for the whole process -- and the hook still fires at exit on an object the user finished with long ago.
shapes.guarded_twin: Very often in the SAME function: a sibling process-level hook that IS reversed -- a signal handler saved with `signal.getsignal` and restored on teardown. One function installs two hooks and undoes one.
shapes.hunt: Grep `atexit.register`, then grep `atexit.unregister` -- the second returning nothing is the finding. MEASURE it: build N objects, `del` them, `gc.collect()`, and count surviving instances via `gc.get_objects()`; `gc.get_referrers` will name the bound method. Then ask whether the exit hook is still CORRECT on a stale object, which is usually the sharper problem.
shapes.expected: an object's process-level registrations are reversed when it is finished with.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT for a short-lived process. It surfaces in long-lived hosts that construct the object repeatedly -- a test runner, a notebook kernel, a worker that reloads config -- as growth plus surprising exit-time behaviour from an object nobody is using.
confirmed_examples: CRF-COVPY-0064 -- coverage.py control.py:654 `atexit.register(self._atexit)` with `atexit.unregister` nowhere in the package; 5/5 Coverage objects survive del+gc.collect(), referrers naming the bound method. Seven lines below, :661 saves the old SIGTERM handler and :761 restores it
references: atexit.unregister exists precisely for this and is rarely reached for
shapes.differential: A module-level singleton that is meant to live for the process is not this shape. It needs an object with a lifecycle shorter than the process -- one the API invites you to create more than once.

shapes.title: State written under a lock at most sites is written (or iterated) without it at another
shapes.pattern: A class attribute or module global is accessed with lock L held at most of its sites (`with self._lock: self._items[k] = v`), but one method writes, mutates or iterates it without L. The lock's purpose is visible in the majority; the outlier breaks it.
shapes.guarded_twin: The other sites: take the same lock around the access, or call the access only from a `_locked` helper that every caller enters with the lock held (and say so in its docstring).
shapes.hunt: For every lock attribute, list the attributes accessed inside its `with` blocks, then grep every other access to those attributes. Helpers called only under the lock are fine; a helper also called from an unlocked path is the defect.
shapes.expected: every write to guarded state happens with its guard held; readers that iterate hold it too.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- lost updates, torn multi-field updates, or `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` under load; never reproduces in single-threaded tests.
references: ft-review-toolkit shared-state-auditor (critical-section inference), ported to Python
threading docs, 'Lock Objects'
shapes.differential: Writes in `__init__` (the object isn't shared yet) are not sites. A plain read of a reference under the GIL is atomic and not flagged. A deliberately racy flag (`self._closed = True`) is benign if every reader tolerates staleness: check the readers.

shapes.title: Lazy init or check-then-insert on shared state without holding the lock across check and act
shapes.pattern: `if self._x is None: self._x = build()` or `if k not in self._cache: self._cache[k] = make()` on state that other code guards with a lock, executed without it. Two threads both see the empty state and both act.
shapes.guarded_twin: Double-checked locking: check, take the lock, re-check, act. Or an atomic primitive: `dict.setdefault`, `functools.cache` on a module function, building in `__init__`.
shapes.hunt: Grep for `is None:` and `not in self.` guards on attributes that also appear inside `with <lock>:` blocks; the unlocked twin is usually in a getter.
shapes.expected: the expensive object is built once, and every thread sees the same instance.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- two instances get built (double connections, leaked worker processes, a cache entry overwritten with a different object that other threads already hold).
references: Python FAQ, 'What kinds of global value mutation are thread-safe?'
shapes.differential: Harmless when building twice is idempotent and cheap and nobody keeps a reference to the loser. Reported `low` when the owning class has a lock but this attribute is never touched under it.

shapes.title: `lock.acquire()` not paired with a `release()` in `finally`
shapes.pattern: `lock.acquire()` followed by work and `lock.release()` on the success path only. An exception (including `KeyboardInterrupt` or a cancellation) between them leaves the lock held forever.
shapes.guarded_twin: `with lock:`; or `lock.acquire()` immediately followed by `try: ... finally: lock.release()`.
shapes.hunt: Grep `.acquire(` and check each for a `finally` release in the same function. An acquire whose release is in another function (a hand-off) needs that function checked on every exit path.
shapes.expected: the lock is released on every exit path.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT until the exceptional path runs; then every later caller deadlocks.
references: ft-review-toolkit scan_lock_discipline (missing release on error path), ported
shapes.differential: `__enter__`/`acquire` methods of a lock wrapper (the protocol itself) and `@contextmanager` bodies that release in `finally` are not defects. A release in another function is reported `low`: follow the hand-off.

shapes.title: `acquire(timeout=...)` / `acquire(False)` whose result is discarded
shapes.pattern: `lock.acquire(timeout=5)` as a bare statement. On timeout it returns False and the code runs the critical section unlocked, then releases a lock it doesn't hold.
shapes.guarded_twin: `if not lock.acquire(timeout=5): raise TimeoutError(...)`, then try/finally.
shapes.hunt: Grep `acquire(` with `timeout=`, `blocking=False` or a positional False; check the return value is tested.
shapes.expected: the timeout path is handled explicitly.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- unlocked access on the timeout path, then `RuntimeError: release unlocked lock` (or a release of another thread's acquisition on a Semaphore).
references: threading docs, Lock.acquire return value
shapes.differential: `acquire(True)` and `acquire()` block until acquired; their result is always True.

shapes.title: Two locks acquired in opposite orders on different paths (deadlock)
shapes.pattern: Path 1 holds A and then takes B; path 2 holds B and then takes A. Either directly (nested `with`) or through calls: a method holding A calls a helper that takes B.
shapes.guarded_twin: One documented global order (e.g. sort per-key locks by key before taking them), or merge the locks.
shapes.hunt: Build the lock-order graph from nested `with` blocks and from calls made while holding a lock; any cycle is a candidate. Check the `chain` of each edge: a weak call edge (method resolved by name only) may not be real.
shapes.expected: all paths take shared locks in one order.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- an intermittent hang under concurrent load, two threads each waiting on the other.
references: ft-review-toolkit scan_lock_discipline (lock-order graph), ported
shapes.differential: Edges through weak (name-only) call resolution are reported `low`. Two instances of one lock family (per-collection locks) nested is an ordering question only if two threads can nest them in opposite orders.

shapes.title: A non-reentrant lock re-acquired by the thread that holds it, or a read-to-write upgrade
shapes.pattern: A method holding `self._lock` (a `threading.Lock`, a `Semaphore`, or a `Condition(Lock())`) calls a helper that takes `self._lock` again; or code holding a reader/writer lock's read side asks for its write side.
shapes.guarded_twin: Split a `_locked` helper that assumes the lock is held; use an `RLock` when re-entry is intended; for RW locks, release the read side before taking the write side (and re-validate).
shapes.hunt: For every `Lock` attribute, follow calls made while it is held (same instance: `self.` calls) to any acquisition of the same attribute.
shapes.expected: a thread never waits for a lock it holds.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- an immediate, permanent self-deadlock on that path, often an error or maintenance path no test exercises.
references: threading docs, 'RLock Objects'
shapes.differential: `RLock`, a default `Condition()` (wraps an RLock), and project RW locks that track their owner thread (`get_ident`) allow re-entry; only their read-to-write upgrade is flagged. A call on another instance (`self.parent.m()`) takes a different lock.

shapes.title: `Condition.wait()` not inside a `while <predicate>` loop
shapes.pattern: `with cv: if not ready: cv.wait()` then proceeds. Wakeups can be spurious, and another consumer can take the item between notify and wake.
shapes.guarded_twin: `while not predicate: cv.wait()`, or `cv.wait_for(predicate)`.
shapes.hunt: Grep `.wait(` on Condition objects; each must sit inside a `while` that re-tests the state.
shapes.expected: the waiter proceeds only when its predicate holds.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- an IndexError/None from an empty queue, or work done on a stale state, under contention only.
references: threading docs, 'Condition Objects' (spurious wakeups)
shapes.differential: `Event.wait()` and `wait(timeout)` used as a sleep are not conditions; the scanner only matches attributes built from `Condition(...)` or named like one (`_cv`, `cond`).

shapes.title: `Condition.notify()` called without holding the condition's lock
shapes.pattern: `cv.notify_all()` outside `with cv:`.
shapes.guarded_twin: Change the shared state and notify inside the same `with cv:` block.
shapes.hunt: Grep `.notify(` / `.notify_all(`; each must be inside `with <that condition>`, or in a helper only called with it held.
shapes.expected: waiters observe the state change that triggered the notify.
shapes.caught_as: `RuntimeError: cannot notify on un-acquired lock` at runtime (threading); lost wakeups for hand-rolled variants.
references: threading docs, Condition.notify
shapes.differential: A helper called only with the condition held (entry lockset) is fine.

shapes.title: Sleep, I/O, a subprocess or a wait on another thread while holding a lock
shapes.pattern: Inside `with lock:` (directly or through calls): `time.sleep`, network or subprocess calls, `thread.join()`, `future.result()`, `queue.get()`, `event.wait()`, file I/O. Every thread that needs the lock waits for the slow work, and waiting on another thread under a lock deadlocks if that thread needs the lock.
shapes.guarded_twin: Compute outside the lock, then lock only to publish the result. Hoist embedding/IO/model work before the lock (a sibling path that already does is the guarded twin).
shapes.hunt: Follow the `chain` of each finding. Look for the same operation on a sibling path that already does the slow work before taking the lock.
shapes.expected: critical sections are short and never wait on other threads.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- throughput collapse and tail-latency spikes under load; deadlock when the awaited thread needs the same lock.
references: ft-review-toolkit scan_stw_safety (unsafe calls in a critical region), ported
shapes.differential: Locks whose purpose is to serialize the slow operation (one writer per file, one request per pipe) are by design: CONSIDER, and check the timeout story instead. File I/O and pipe waits are reported `low` for this reason.

shapes.title: `await` inside a sync `with <threading lock>` block
shapes.pattern: `with self._lock: ... await something()` in an `async def`. The coroutine suspends holding a thread lock; any other task on the loop that takes the lock blocks the loop thread, and the holder can never resume.
shapes.guarded_twin: `asyncio.Lock` with `async with`, or release before awaiting.
shapes.hunt: Grep `async def` bodies for sync `with` blocks on locks that contain `await`.
shapes.expected: no thread lock is held across a suspension point.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- the whole event loop freezes the first time two tasks contend.
references: asyncio docs, 'Synchronization Primitives' (not thread-safe, and vice versa)
shapes.differential: None for threading locks. An `asyncio.Lock` (with `async with`) is the guarded twin.

shapes.title: `async def` calls a sync project function that blocks or waits for a slow thread lock
shapes.pattern: A coroutine calls a sync function inline (not via `to_thread`/`run_in_executor`), and that function -- possibly several calls down -- sleeps, does network or subprocess work, or takes a thread lock that other code holds across blocking work. `blocking-call-in-async-function` misses it because no blocking name appears in the coroutine.
shapes.guarded_twin: `await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...)` / `await loop.run_in_executor(None, fn)`. A sibling coroutine in the same module that already offloads its sync call is the guarded twin, and raises confidence.
shapes.hunt: For each `async def`, list its inline calls to sync project functions and follow them to a lock or a blocking call. Then ask which other code holds that lock, and for how long (the finding's `meanwhile` hop).
shapes.expected: the event loop never waits on another thread's critical section.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- the whole server (health checks included) stops answering while another thread holds the lock, e.g. for the duration of a restore.
references: asyncio developer guide, 'Running Blocking Code'
ft-review-toolkit scan_stw_safety (unsafe-call propagation through an intra-file call graph), ported
shapes.differential: A lock that is only ever held for a few bytecodes (counters) costs microseconds: reported `low`. Startup/shutdown code before the server accepts requests is usually acceptable.

shapes.title: A `signal.signal` handler that takes locks, logs or does I/O
shapes.pattern: A handler registered with `signal.signal` acquires a lock, logs, or does I/O. Python runs it between two bytecodes of the main thread, which may already hold that lock -- including the `logging` module's handler locks.
shapes.guarded_twin: Set a flag or write a byte to a self-pipe (`signal.set_wakeup_fd`, `loop.add_signal_handler`), and do the work in the main loop.
shapes.hunt: Find every `signal.signal(..., handler)` and read the handler and what it calls.
shapes.expected: the handler returns immediately without touching shared locks.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- a rare deadlock when the signal lands while the main thread holds the lock (often in logging).
references: Python docs, 'signal -- Note on signal handlers and exceptions'
shapes.differential: Handlers that only log are CONSIDER: the deadlock needs the main thread to be inside the same handler's lock. `loop.add_signal_handler` callbacks run on the loop, not in signal context.

shapes.title: A request/reply channel without request ids, retried or reused after a timeout
shapes.pattern: `conn.send(req); if not conn.poll(timeout): raise/retry; reply = conn.recv()` over a pipe, socket or queue shared across calls, with no request id in the reply. After a timeout the late reply stays in the channel, and the next caller receives the previous caller's answer -- forever after, every reply is shifted by one.
shapes.guarded_twin: Tag each request with an id and discard replies whose id doesn't match; or tear down and recreate the channel (or the worker) on every timeout path, including the last retry.
shapes.hunt: Find every send/poll/recv sequence; check what happens to the channel on each timeout or exception path, especially the final attempt of a retry loop.
shapes.expected: a timed-out request's reply can never be returned to a later request.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT -- plausible but wrong results (here, another tenant's embeddings), with no error.
references: multiprocessing docs, Connection.poll/recv
the response-desync bug class of pipelined HTTP/1.1 and Redis clients
shapes.differential: Channels recreated on every failure, or protocols that carry and check a correlation id, are the guarded twin.

shapes.title: Post-success cleanup inside the `try` whose `except` rolls the operation back
shapes.pattern: `try: move_old_aside(); install_new(); remove_backup()` / `except: rollback()`. The last statement is cleanup after a fully successful operation, but it sits inside the `try`, so a cleanup failure (an undeletable file, EBUSY on NFS) runs the rollback: the new state is removed, and a partly-completed cleanup (rmtree deletes as it goes) has already destroyed part of the backup the rollback needs.
shapes.guarded_twin: Cleanup after the `try`/`except`, in its own `try` that only logs: `try: remove_backup() except OSError: log.warning(...)`. A sibling operation in the same codebase that already does this is the twin.
shapes.hunt: In every `try` whose `except` performs rollback (restore, rename back, delete what was installed), read the last statements of the `try` body: `rmtree`, `unlink`, temp-file or backup removal belongs after it.
shapes.expected: a cleanup failure after success leaves the success in place and is reported as a warning.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT until the environment refuses the cleanup; then a successful operation is reported as failed, and both the old and new state can be lost.
references: shutil.rmtree docs (deletes as it walks; a failure leaves a partial tree)
shapes.differential: Cleanup that is itself part of the operation's atomicity (removing a lock file that other processes check) may belong inside. Check whether the rollback can survive a half-done cleanup.

shapes.title: Logging, metrics or audit I/O in a `finally` (or after the commit) that can raise
shapes.pattern: `try: result = do_write() finally: audit_log.write(event)`. If the side-channel call raises (disk full, closed handle, a metrics backend error), the exception replaces the function's return value -- or the original exception -- so a committed write answers as a failure, or the real error is lost.
shapes.guarded_twin: Side-channel calls are total: wrapped in their own `try/except Exception` that counts or logs at most once, or routed through a helper that never raises. The project's other observability helpers that already swallow their own errors are the twin.
shapes.hunt: List every `finally:` block and every statement after a commit point; for each logging/metrics/audit call there, ask what happens if it raises. Then check the side channel's own configure/flush/close paths.
shapes.expected: observability failures never change the data plane's result or mask its exception.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT in tests (the side channel works there); in production a full log volume turns successful requests into 500s and hides the original exception.
references: Python docs, 'try statement' (an exception in finally replaces the pending one)
shapes.differential: Standard `logging` handlers already catch their own errors (`Handler.handleError`); the shape is about project-owned writers, metrics clients and audit logs that don't.

shapes.title: A linter's 'safe' autofix removes an `except ... as NAME` binding that a closure still uses
shapes.pattern: `except Exception as exc: retry(lambda c: c.fail(error=str(exc))); raise`. Some linters (ruff F841/F821, pyflakes) don't see the use inside the lambda/nested def, report `exc` as unused and undefined, and offer a *safe* fix that deletes `as exc`. After the fix the closure raises NameError on the error path -- the path tests rarely exercise.
shapes.guarded_twin: Bind the value outside the closure (`message = str(exc)` before the lambda), or pass it as a default argument (`lambda c, msg=str(exc): ...`). Either keeps the code correct under the autofix and silences the false positive.
shapes.hunt: For each F841 on an `except ... as NAME` line, look for NAME inside a lambda or nested def in the same handler; the matching F821 at that use is the co-signal. Never recommend the autofix for these; also check whether whole-project `--fix` runs elsewhere (pre-commit, CI).
shapes.expected: error-handling code keeps working after the project's own lint autofix.
shapes.caught_as: SILENT until someone runs the autofix; then the error path raises NameError instead of reporting the original failure, and the test suite usually still passes.
references: ruff issue #6878 (F841/F821 false positive on exception names used in nested functions)
pyflakes issue #265
shapes.differential: An `except ... as NAME` whose NAME is really unused anywhere (no closure) is a genuine F841; the fix is safe there.
